title: The bitter fruit made sweet
hookLine: tradition says a hungry Mardana ate bitter soapnuts at Nanak's word and found them sweet

lines: BITTER ENOUGH TO FOLD A FACE.
A HUNGRY MAN, THE WRONG TREE.
cards: Soapnuts. Some people still use them for laundry: small brown shells, dropped into a cloth bag and tossed in the wash, and they foam like soap. They aren't food.

They're bitter enough to make a whole face fold up. Hold on to that, because in today's sakhi, a starving man is told to eat them. Mardana is in the hills, hungry again, and the only food in sight grows on the wrong tree.

teach.b: In the tellings, Nanak and Mardana are walking through wild hill country, far from any village. Mardana is hungry, and says so, the way he does more than once in these stories.
He's the very human one on the road, the one who gets tired and wants his dinner.
Nanak points to a tree: a reetha, a soapnut tree. Eat, he says. Mardana hesitates.
Soapnuts are bitter, and he knows it. But he trusts the Guru, picks one, and bites.
And tradition says it was sweet, sweet enough to fill him. Tradition links a gurdwara in those hills to this story, and it carries the tree's name. What does the story know?
Something about hunger and about trust. Mardana doesn't get a feast. He gets the plain thing in front of him, the thing he'd have walked past, and it's the Guru's word that changes the taste.
The Gurus' hymns speak of the Name as sweet. They speak of accepting what comes as the sweet will of God. So the sakhi turns that teaching into fruit.

teach.h: THE SAME BITE, BITTER OR SWEET.
teach.b: However the wonder is held, the scene makes a plain point: the same bite can taste bitter or sweet depending on what's brought to it. Met with complaint, it's soap.
Received with thanks, in the Guru's name, it fed a hungry man.
The sakhi doesn't ask Mardana to pretend the fruit isn't bitter. It asks him to take one bite.

how: Sikhs tell the reetha sakhi as a story of trust and gratitude, and tradition links a gurdwara in the hills, named for the reetha tree, to it.

o: a sacred tree planted by the Guru himself
a sweet mango that grows wild in the hills
the bitter soapnut Mardana ate at the Guru's word

games.q: inside the sakhi — tap the pairs.

s: soapnuts are a sweet fruit people normally eat
they're bitter and used like soap. that's what makes the sakhi surprising.
Mardana ate at the Guru's word, despite knowing the fruit was bitter
he trusted, bit, and tradition says it was sweet.
the sakhi gives Mardana a feast
he gets the plain thing in front of him, and it feeds him.

games.q: you're Mardana. you're starving in the hills, and the Guru points to a soapnut tree and says eat. what do you do?
o: trust him, pick one, and bite.
keep walking and hope for a village.
games.why: he trusted and bit, and tradition says the bitter fruit was sweet.

practice: Take one plain thing if you have it nearby, a piece of bread, a cracker, a glass of water, or simply remember the last plain thing you ate.
Taste it slowly, notice the taste before you judge it, and give thanks for it, out loud or inside, as if it were the best thing on the table. If you pray, you can say Waheguru before the first bite.

wordCard.voice: Reetha, the bitter soapnut Mardana ate at the Guru's word, hungry in the hills, and tradition says it was sweet.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: the soapnut, the bitter fruit of today's sakhi.

carryVoice: Your line: bitter made sweet. The same bite, met with thanks, fed a hungry man. See you tomorrow.
